job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

response.passage: In the bustling city of Vidyut Nagar, engineers recently repaired the town’s main street lighting system. During the inspection, they explained how a simple circuit works to keep the streets bright. A bulb glows only when a complete, unbroken path exists from one terminal of the electric cell to the other. Specifically, one wire must connect to the metal tip at the base of the bulb, while the second wire must touch the metal casing surrounding the base. Contrary to popular belief, electricity does not get 'used up' by the bulb; the same amount of current that enters the filament returns to the cell. The engineers also clarified that while metals are excellent conductors, some materials like damp wood or salty water can also allow current to pass, proving that not all non-metals are perfect insulators. Finally, they demonstrated that for two cells to power a torch, the positive terminal of one must touch the negative terminal of the other. If they are placed facing the same direction, the circuit remains incomplete, and the bulb will not glow. The light is produced by the glowing filament inside, not the glass cover itself.
response.summary: A working circuit requires a complete path connecting both bulb terminals to the cell. Electricity is conserved throughout the circuit, and proper cell orientation is essential for functionality.
